known_defects.summary: COMMENTS ARE NOT NESTED. They arrive as separate dataset rows with `type: "comment"`, and almost every field differs from a post: the author is `actor` not `author`, the headline is `actor.position` not `author.info`, the text is `commentary` not `content`, and the date is a flat `createdAt` string rather than a `postedAt` object. One run with maxPosts 6 returned 5 posts and 23 comments in one flat dataset.
known_defects.mitigation: `splitPostSearchRows` discriminates on `type` before normalising, and `normalizeSocialComment` reads the comment shape. Read as posts, all 23 comments would have normalised to nulls and been billed anyway.

known_defects.summary: COMMENT QUALITY IS BIMODAL. Of 23 observed comments, roughly a quarter carried real signal — one founder wrote "three email campaigns earlier this summer, not a single reply... I still can't tell you if that's channel, list quality, or us" — while the rest were congratulation noise ("say it louder", "this is seriously useful!!"), self-promotional links, or near-identical AI-written engagement bait: two different accounts posted the same observation about "1 positive reply per 53 emails" in nearly the same words.
known_defects.mitigation: A comment is a CANDIDATE, never intent. The model must read each one for meaning, and near-duplicate comments across accounts must be treated as one low-value signal rather than corroboration.

known_defects.summary: A B2B problem query surfaces the people who SELL the solution. Observed commenter headlines included "Cold Email Specialist", "B2B Lead Generation & Outbound Specialist" and "Sales Automation for Agencies" — practitioners marketing themselves on a thread about the problem they sell against.
known_defects.mitigation: This is exactly why ICP fit is judged SEPARATELY from intent. Someone discussing the problem fluently is often a competitor, and signal alone must never promote a candidate.

known_defects.summary: A COMMENTER's `actor.linkedinUrl` is a clean `/in/handle`. A POST author's `author.linkedinUrl` carries a rotating `miniProfileUrn` query parameter. The same person can therefore appear under two different URLs depending on which row they came from.
known_defects.mitigation: Both normalizers strip the query string, and identity keys on the opaque `ACoAAA…` member id, which is stable across both shapes.

known_defects.summary: `actor.author` is a boolean marking whether the commenter is the post's own author replying in their thread.
known_defects.mitigation: Carried as `is_post_author`. An author replying to their own post is not third-party engagement and should not be counted as one.

known_defects.summary: Comments are billed at the SAME price as posts. maxPosts 50 with maxComments 10 is up to 550 billable items, not 50.
known_defects.mitigation: The compiler caps posts and comments separately and states the multiplied worst case in the cost estimate.

known_defects.summary: `authorKeywords` matches the author's self-written headline. A headline saying CEO is a claim by that person, not verified employment.
known_defects.mitigation: A person-subject claim from this Actor is corroboration. Employer verification remains the existing people-stage contract.

known_defects.summary: LinkedIn full-text relevance decides what matches, not a topic model. A post can match a query without being about the topic.
known_defects.mitigation: The topic qualifier is re-checked against post text during qualification; a search match alone never satisfies a topic requirement.

request_bounds_basis.details: The actor bills per company looked up, and both `companies[]` (URLs) and `searches[]` (names to search) are looked up (experiments/hiring-actor-benchmark-2026-08-01/schemas/harvestapi__linkedin-company.input.json; compileHarvestCompanyDetailsInput bills companies + searches). The engine sends one LinkedIn URL in `companies` and never `searches`, so `searches` is refused outright and the purchase is one company.
request_bounds_basis.jobs: Billed rows are maxItems per job title per location: the actor runs once per `jobTitles` entry, and maxItems applies per title and location input (harvestapi__linkedin-job-search.input.json). `jobTitles`, `locations` and `geoIds` (the other location filter) are therefore bounded, and `maxItems` is mandatory. `company`, `industryIds`, `workplaceType`, `employmentType`, `experienceLevel`, `salary`, `postedLimit`, `sortBy`, `under10Applicants` and `easyApply` are filters that narrow each search, and `page` only chooses where a search starts, so none of them multiplies the rows. They are left unbounded, and the gate-pinned maxTotalChargeUsd caps the run either way.
